demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is fifty-six now, a European man who has spent most of his life inside studios and theaters, teaching his body to tell stories before words arrive. He is married, and for decades dancing has given shape to his days: class in the morning, rehearsals in the afternoon, performances or coaching in the evening. He describes himself as someone who has always trusted movement. Before the accident, he says, he could walk into a room and know where every limb belonged.

The event happens during a rehearsal nearly two years ago. He is working with a younger guest artist on a partnered sequence he has done in some form hundreds of times. The floor is slightly tackier than usual from a recent cleaning, though no one says much about it. They run the lift again and again, trying to find a cleaner line. On one attempt, he adjusts his grip mid-motion. He feels his right foot drag a fraction of a second behind where it should be. The timing goes wrong. Her weight shifts outside his center. He cannot recover. She falls awkwardly, and the sound her body makes when it hits the floor is what stays with him most. He says it is not loud in memory, just final.

In the first moments afterward, he goes cold and strangely precise. He kneels beside her, hears himself asking if she can move, hears the stage manager calling emergency services, sees the faces around him sharpen with alarm. At the hospital he learns she has suffered multiple fractures and a spinal injury requiring surgery. Nobody tells him directly that it is his fault, but he does not need them to. He repeats the sequence to himself all night in the plastic chair beside his wife: the grip, the floor, the hesitation, the drop. By morning, the story has settled into something simple and punishing-he did this.

In the weeks after, he stops dancing abruptly. At first he calls it a pause, a respectful distance while she recovers. He sends flowers, then rewrites the card three times because every version sounds either self-excusing or unbearable. When colleagues text, he reads the messages and leaves them unanswered. He tells his wife he is tired, but what he means is that he cannot enter a studio without feeling the fall begin again in his body. If music comes on unexpectedly, he feels his stomach tighten. When he closes his eyes to sleep, he sees her leaving his hands. He begins delaying bedtime because night is when the replay starts. When he does sleep, he wakes with his heart pounding, his arms jerking as if trying too late to catch her.

His wife notices he no longer reaches for her in bed. He starts taking long routes through the city to avoid the theater district. On mornings when he has to pass the company building, he feels sweat gather under his shirt before he even turns the corner. Once, hearing a dancer backstage shout after missing a landing in another rehearsal room, he drops to a crouch before he understands where he is. He is embarrassed by the intensity of it and angrier still that his body seems to know only one story now.

He tries returning to work in smaller ways. He agrees to coach from the side rather than demonstrate. But even watching partnering rehearsals leaves him rigid, scanning feet, wrists, spacing, every possible point of failure. He interrupts constantly: too high, too fast, again, stop. Younger dancers begin to look at him warily. He goes home ashamed, hearing his own voice as clipped and brittle. The generous teacher he once was feels far away. He says that before the accident he used to watch dance for beauty; now he watches for catastrophe.

At home, his world narrows. His wife suggests dinner with friends, and he refuses because he cannot bear the moment people soften their faces and ask how he is doing. He keeps meaning to call the injured dancer but rehearses the conversation until it becomes impossible. Some days he searches her name online, looking for signs of recovery, then feels sick for intruding. He carries a steady conviction that he has forfeited the right to joy. When his wife laughs at something on television, he finds himself irritated, then immediately disgusted with himself.

He speaks often about guilt, but underneath it there is fear he is slower to name. He no longer trusts his body. In class, if he demonstrates even a simple turn, he feels a flash of unreality, as if the room has thinned and he is watching himself from a distance. He avoids lifts entirely. He has begun startling at dropped objects, ambulance sirens, the thud of someone jumping from a platform. His concentration frays. Reading choreography notes, he reaches the bottom of the page and realizes he has been back in that rehearsal the whole time.

Now, nearly two years later, his life is organized around not letting that moment happen again, though it already has. He still loves dance with a kind of grief in it. He still goes to the studio, but he stands near the wall, alert and tired, as if bracing for impact. He says the worst part is that the accident lasts only seconds, yet it has entered every hour that follows.
